svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. The 2022 vault breach, and the three decisions that made it worse
svg.desc: A case study. Encrypted vault backups were taken. Three prior design decisions turned that into vault compromise for many users: legacy accounts were never migrated to a higher key derivation work factor, some fields including site addresses were stored unencrypted, and the vault is a single durable blob that does not change when a password is rotated. The consequences followed years later, including linked cryptocurrency thefts and a class action settlement.
svg.text: Figure 2: What a Vault Breach Actually Costs
The most instructive incident available to this topic, and most course material gives it a footnote.
2022: attackers exfiltrate backup copies of customer vaults
The vaults were encrypted, which is what the architecture promised. Everything that follows is about what that promise did and did not cover.
Three decisions made years earlier, which decided the outcome

g.text: The work factor protecting a vault was
raised for new accounts over the years.
Existing accounts were never moved,
despite a commitment to do so.
Many were still at five thousand rounds.
Some were found at five hundred.
A default improved is not a default applied.

svg.text: Not all of it was encrypted

g.text: Usernames and passwords were encrypted.
Some fields were not, including the
addresses of the sites each entry was for.
So before cracking anything, an attacker
could sort the stolen vaults by which ones
held accounts worth the effort.
Metadata again, deciding who gets targeted.
A stolen copy stays valid for as long as
its contents do. There is no equivalent of
forward secrecy for a password vault.
Anything in it that cannot be rotated,
such as a recovery phrase or an answer to
a security question, is exposed forever.
Rotating a password does not recall a copy.
Researchers linked a series of cryptocurrency thefts to the breach, with a common factor among victims: recovery phrases kept in the vault.
Federal investigators later attributed a much larger theft to the same stolen data. A class action was settled in 2025.
The gap between the breach and the losses was measured in years, because offline cracking has no deadline.

svg.text: Three things to take from this, and none of them is "avoid one vendor"
Check the work factor on your own vault rather than trusting the current default. Assume everything not explicitly encrypted is readable. And keep anything
unrotatable out of the vault entirely, because a stolen copy of it never expires.
